One-degree global ocean–sea ice OMIP-style simulation

This example configures a global ocean–sea ice simulation on the 1ᵒ NEMO eORCA1 grid, in a configuration similar to the Ocean Model Intercomparison Project (OMIP) protocol of Griffies et al. (2016): 100 vertical levels, CATKE vertical mixing over a uniform background diffusivity, Gent-McWilliams and Redi isopycnal mixing discretized on Griffies triads, and a biharmonic viscosity. The simulation is forced by repeat-year JRA55 atmospheric reanalysis, its surface salinity is restored to the World Ocean Atlas monthly climatology, and it is initialized by World Ocean Atlas temperature and salinity and by ECCO sea ice concentration and thickness.

For this example, we need Oceananigans, NumericalEarth, ClimaSeaIce, WorldOceanAtlasTools, Dates, CUDA, and CairoMakie to visualize the simulation.

using NumericalEarth
using Oceananigans
using Oceananigans.Units
using ClimaSeaIce: IncrementalRemapping, ConductiveFlux, UniformThicknessDistribution
using WorldOceanAtlasTools
using Dates
using Printf
using Statistics
using CUDA
[ Info: Oceananigans will use 8 threads

Grid and Bathymetry

The horizontal grid and the bathymetry come from the NEMO eORCA1 mesh, of which we keep only the largest connected basin. In the vertical we use 100 levels whose spacing grows by 7.49% per level from 1.5 m at the surface until it reaches 100 m at about 1400 m depth, so that the 100 levels span 5500 m.

arch = GPU()

top_cell_thickness = 1.5          # m

z = ReferenceToStretchedDiscretization(extent = 5500,
                                       constant_spacing = top_cell_thickness,
                                       constant_spacing_extent = top_cell_thickness,
                                       maximum_spacing = 100,
                                       stretching = LinearStretching(0.0749),
                                       rounding_digits = 4,
                                       mutable = true)

grid = ORCAGrid(arch; dataset = ORCAOne(), Nz = 100, z, halo = (8, 8, 8), major_basins = 1)
360×296×100 ImmersedBoundaryGrid{Float64, Periodic, TwoSided{Closed, FaceFolded}, Bounded} on CUDAGPU with 8×8×8 halo:
├── immersed_boundary: GridFittedBottom(mean(z)=-2085.62, min(z)=-5500.11, max(z)=0.0)
├── underlying_grid: 360×296×100 OrthogonalSphericalShellGrid{Float64, Periodic, TwoSided{Closed, FaceFolded}, Bounded} on CUDAGPU with 8×8×8 halo
├── centered at (λ, φ) = (-107.0, -1.1665)
├── longitude: Periodic  extent 360.011 degrees                     variably spaced with min(Δλ)=8.99322e-6, max(Δλ)=1.00003
├── latitude:  TwoSided{Closed, FaceFolded}  extent 169.544 degrees variably spaced with min(Δφ)=8.99322e-6, max(Δφ)=0.947843
└── z:         Bounded  z ∈ [-5500.11, 0.0]                         variably and mutably spaced with min(Δr)=1.5, max(Δr)=100.0

Closures

Vertical mixing is CATKE (Wagner et al., 2025), on top of a uniform background diffusivity $κ$ = 10⁻⁵ m² s⁻¹ and viscosity $ν$ = 3 × 10⁻⁵ m² s⁻¹. The mesoscale eddy fluxes are parameterized with a Gent and McWilliams (1990) skew diffusivity of 500 m² s⁻¹ and a Redi (1982) isopycnal diffusivity of 800 m² s⁻¹, both discretized with the triads of Griffies et al. (1998) and Griffies (1998). Finally, a biharmonic viscosity $ν = A_z^2 / λ$ damps grid-scale motions on a timescale $λ$ = 50 days independently of the cell area $A_z$.

using Oceananigans.TurbulenceClosures: IsopycnalSkewSymmetricDiffusivity, ScalarBiharmonicDiffusivity
using Oceananigans.TurbulenceClosures.TKEBasedVerticalDiffusivities: CATKEMixingLength
using Oceananigans.Operators: Az

vertical_mixing = CATKEVerticalDiffusivity(VerticallyImplicitTimeDiscretization();
                                           mixing_length = CATKEMixingLength(Cᵇ = 0.01),
                                           maximum_viscosity = 3,
                                           maximum_tracer_diffusivity = 3,
                                           maximum_tke_diffusivity = 3,
                                           negative_tke_damping_time_scale = 10)

background_mixing = VerticalScalarDiffusivity(κ = 1e-5, ν = 3e-5)

eddy_closure = IsopycnalSkewSymmetricDiffusivity(κ_skew = 500, κ_symmetric = 800)

@inline biharmonic_viscosity(i, j, k, grid, ℓx, ℓy, ℓz, clock, fields, λ) = Az(i, j, k, grid, ℓx, ℓy, ℓz)^2 / λ

horizontal_viscosity = HorizontalScalarBiharmonicDiffusivity(ν = biharmonic_viscosity,
                                                             discrete_form = true,
                                                             parameters = 50days)
ScalarBiharmonicDiffusivity{HorizontalFormulation}(ν=Oceananigans.TurbulenceClosures.DiscreteDiffusionFunction{Nothing, Nothing, Nothing, Float64, typeof(Main.var"##277".biharmonic_viscosity)}, κ=nothing)

Land

The river and iceberg runoff of JRA55-do (Tsujino et al., 2018) is spread over the eight wet cells closest to each river mouth. We build the land before the ocean, so that the ocean can enhance the vertical mixing at the river mouths.

land = JRA55PrescribedLand(grid; spread_radius = nothing, maximum_spread_cells = 8)
1440×720×1×365 PrescribedLand on LatitudeLongitudeGrid:
├── times: 365-element StepRangeLen{Float64, Base.TwicePrecision{Float64}, Base.TwicePrecision{Float64}, Int64}
└── freshwater_flux: (:rivers, :icebergs)

Ocean simulation

The penetrating shortwave radiation is absorbed in two bands, whose attenuation follows the SeaWiFS monthly chlorophyll climatology, cycled every year, as in Manizza et al. (2005). The surface salinity is restored to the World Ocean Atlas monthly climatology with a piston velocity of 0.254 m day⁻¹, which over the 1.5 m top cell corresponds to a restoring rate of 0.254 / 1.5 day⁻¹. The restoring is applied as a surface salt flux whose global mean is removed, so that it neither adds nor removes salt.

using NumericalEarth.DataWrangling: SeaWiFSMonthly,
                                    SurfaceFluxRestoring,
                                    ConservativeSurfaceFluxRestoring,
                                    ConservativeSurfaceFluxRestoringCallback

chlorophyll_dates    = (DateTime(2000, 1, 1), DateTime(2000, 12, 1))
chlorophyll_metadata = Metadata(:chlorophyll; dataset = SeaWiFSMonthly(), dates = chlorophyll_dates)
chlorophyll          = FieldTimeSeries(chlorophyll_metadata, grid)
radiative_forcing    = TwoColorRadiation(grid; chlorophyll)

piston_velocity    = 0.254 / days # m s⁻¹

salinity_restoring = DatasetRestoring(Metadata(:salinity; dataset = WOAMonthly()), arch;
                                      rate = piston_velocity / top_cell_thickness,
                                      time_indices_in_memory = 12)

salinity_flux = ConservativeSurfaceFluxRestoring(SurfaceFluxRestoring(salinity_restoring), grid)

We use a split-explicit free surface with 300 barotropic substeps, fifth-order WENO for momentum and seventh-order WENO for tracers. Both treat vertical advection implicitly wherever the vertical Courant number exceeds one.

time_discretization = AdaptiveVerticallyImplicitDiscretization(cfl = 1)

free_surface       = SplitExplicitFreeSurface(grid; substeps = 300)
momentum_advection = WENOVectorInvariant(order = 5; time_discretization)
tracer_advection   = WENO(order = 7; time_discretization)

ocean = ocean_simulation(grid; momentum_advection, tracer_advection, free_surface, radiative_forcing,
                         reference_density = 1026,
                         closure = (vertical_mixing, eddy_closure, horizontal_viscosity, background_mixing),
                         river_routing = land.river_routing,
                         additional_surface_fluxes = (; S = salinity_flux))

Sea Ice simulation

The sea ice has the elastic–viscous–plastic (EVP) rheology of Hunke and Dukowicz (1997), a snow layer over a slab of ice, and is advected by the incremental remapping of Lipscomb and Hunke (2004). The ice–ocean drag is computed against the ocean velocity averaged over the top 6 m. Heat is conducted through the snow and the ice as if each were spread uniformly over four sub-grid categories, which raises the effective conductivity of both by a factor $1 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7$.

dynamics = NumericalEarth.SeaIces.sea_ice_dynamics(grid, ocean; sea_ice_ocean_drag_reference_depth = 6)

itd_shape = UniformThicknessDistribution(categories = 4)
internal_heat_flux  = ConductiveFlux(; conductivity = 2, itd_shape)
snow_thermodynamics = NumericalEarth.SeaIces.default_snow_thermodynamics(grid; itd_shape)

sea_ice = sea_ice_simulation(grid, ocean; dynamics, internal_heat_flux, snow_thermodynamics,
                             advection = IncrementalRemapping())

Initial condition

We initialize the ocean with the World Ocean Atlas annual climatology and the sea ice with the ECCO state estimate of January 1993.

set!(ocean.model, MetadataSet((:temperature, :salinity); dataset = WOAAnnual()))
set!(sea_ice.model, MetadataSet((:sea_ice_thickness, :sea_ice_concentration); dataset = ECCO4Monthly(),
                                date = DateTime(1993, 1, 1)))

JRA55-based atmospheric state and radiation

We force the simulation with the JRA55-do repeat-year atmospheric state and downwelling radiation (Stewart et al., 2020). The ocean has an albedo of 0.06, and the sea ice albedo depends on the ice thickness, the snow thickness, and the surface temperature as in CCSM3 (Briegleb et al., 2004).

atmosphere = JRA55PrescribedAtmosphere(arch)

sea_ice_albedo = SeaIceAlbedo(sea_ice.model.ice_thickness,
                              sea_ice.model.snow_thickness,
                              sea_ice.model.snow_thermodynamics.top_surface_temperature)

ocean_surface   = SurfaceRadiationProperties(0.06, 1)
sea_ice_surface = SurfaceRadiationProperties(sea_ice_albedo, 1)
radiation = JRA55PrescribedRadiation(arch; ocean_surface, sea_ice_surface)

Turbulent fluxes

Over the ocean, the turbulent fluxes follow the OMIP-2 bulk formulae of Large and Yeager (2004) and Large and Yeager (2009), whose transfer coefficients are iterated directly, five times. Over the sea ice, Monin-Obukhov similarity uses the SHEBA stability functions of Grachev et al. (2007) with roughness lengths fixed at 5 × 10⁻⁴ m for momentum and 5 × 10⁻⁵ m for heat and moisture, and a minimum gustiness of 0.2 m s⁻¹. The saturation specific humidity is enhanced by the moist-air factor of Gill (1982) over both the ocean, where it is 98% of the pure-water value, and the sea ice. The ice–ocean heat flux follows the three-equation formulation of Holland and Jenkins (1999), with a friction velocity computed from the ice–ocean stress.

using NumericalEarth.EarthSystemModels: AtmosphericThermodynamics
using NumericalEarth.EarthSystemModels.InterfaceComputations: LargeYeagerTransferCoefficients,
                                                              COARELogarithmicSimilarityProfile,
                                                              ConvectiveGustiness,
                                                              ImpureSaturationSpecificHumidity,
                                                              GillSaturationEnhancement,
                                                              ThreeEquationHeatFlux,
                                                              MomentumBasedFrictionVelocity,
                                                              atmosphere_sea_ice_stability_functions

saturation_enhancement = GillSaturationEnhancement()

atmosphere_ocean_interface_specific_humidity   = ImpureSaturationSpecificHumidity(AtmosphericThermodynamics.Liquid(), 0.98; saturation_enhancement)
atmosphere_sea_ice_interface_specific_humidity = ImpureSaturationSpecificHumidity(AtmosphericThermodynamics.Ice(); saturation_enhancement)

atmosphere_ocean_fluxes = CoefficientBasedFluxes(transfer_coefficients = LargeYeagerTransferCoefficients(),
                                                 solver_stop_criteria = FixedIterations(5))

atmosphere_sea_ice_fluxes = SimilarityTheoryFluxes(stability_functions = atmosphere_sea_ice_stability_functions(),
                                                   similarity_form = COARELogarithmicSimilarityProfile(),
                                                   subgrid_velocities = ConvectiveGustiness(minimum_gustiness = 0.2),
                                                   momentum_roughness_length = 5e-4,
                                                   temperature_roughness_length = 5e-5,
                                                   water_vapor_roughness_length = 5e-5)

sea_ice_ocean_heat_flux = ThreeEquationHeatFlux(sea_ice; heat_transfer_coefficient = 0.0057, friction_velocity = MomentumBasedFrictionVelocity())

Coupled simulation

Now we are ready to build the coupled ocean–sea ice model and bring everything together into a simulation with a 90-minute time step.

coupled_model = OceanSeaIceModel(ocean, sea_ice; atmosphere, land, radiation,
                                 atmosphere_ocean_fluxes, atmosphere_sea_ice_fluxes, sea_ice_ocean_heat_flux,
                                 atmosphere_ocean_interface_specific_humidity,
                                 atmosphere_sea_ice_interface_specific_humidity)

simulation = Simulation(coupled_model; Δt=90minutes, stop_time=90days)

The salinity restoring flux, and with it its global mean, is recomputed from the ocean state every time step.

add_callback!(simulation, ConservativeSurfaceFluxRestoringCallback(salinity_flux, ocean.model))

The prescribed precipitation and runoff do not balance the evaporation, so, as in most OMIP-2 models (Tsujino et al., 2020), we remove the net freshwater imbalance at every time step and hold the total water of the ocean, sea ice, and snow at its initial value.

add_callback!(simulation, TotalWaterNormalization(coupled_model), IterationInterval(1))

A progress messenger

We write a function that prints out a helpful progress message while the simulation runs.

wall_time = Ref(time_ns())

function progress(sim)
    ocean = sim.model.ocean
    u, v, w = ocean.model.velocities
    T = ocean.model.tracers.T
    e = ocean.model.tracers.e
    Tmin, Tmax, Tavg = minimum(T), maximum(T), mean(view(T, :, :, ocean.model.grid.Nz))
    emax = maximum(e)
    umax = (maximum(abs, u), maximum(abs, v), maximum(abs, w))

    step_time = 1e-9 * (time_ns() - wall_time[])

    msg1 = @sprintf("time: %s, iter: %d", prettytime(sim), iteration(sim))
    msg2 = @sprintf(", max|uo|: (%.1e, %.1e, %.1e) m s⁻¹", umax...)
    msg3 = @sprintf(", extrema(To): (%.1f, %.1f) ᵒC, mean(To(z=0)): %.1f ᵒC", Tmin, Tmax, Tavg)
    msg4 = @sprintf(", max(e): %.2f m² s⁻²", emax)
    msg5 = @sprintf(", wall time: %s \n", prettytime(step_time))

    @info msg1 * msg2 * msg3 * msg4 * msg5

    wall_time[] = time_ns()

     return nothing
end
progress (generic function with 1 method)

And add it as a callback to the simulation.

add_callback!(simulation, progress, TimeInterval(5days))

Output

We are almost there! We need to save some output. Below we choose to save only surface fields using the indices keyword argument. We save all the velocity and tracer components. Note, that besides temperature and salinity, the CATKE vertical mixing parameterization also uses a prognostic turbulent kinetic energy, $e$, to diagnose the vertical mixing length.

By default, the writers save the ocean model's Coriolis, buoyancy, and closure to every file. JLD2 cannot store the user-defined biharmonic_viscosity function, so we save the closure ourselves, without the biharmonic viscosity, through the writer's init function.

save_closure_without_biharmonic(file, model) =
    file["serialized/closure"] = filter(c -> !(c isa ScalarBiharmonicDiffusivity), model.closure)

ocean_outputs = merge(ocean.model.tracers, ocean.model.velocities)
free_surface = ocean.model.free_surface.displacement
sea_ice_outputs = merge((h = sea_ice.model.ice_thickness,
                         ℵ = sea_ice.model.ice_concentration,
                         T = sea_ice.model.ice_thermodynamics.top_surface_temperature),
                         sea_ice.model.velocities)

ocean.output_writers[:surface] = JLD2Writer(ocean.model, ocean_outputs;
                                            schedule = TimeInterval(1days),
                                            filename = "ocean_one_degree_surface_fields",
                                            indices = (:, :, grid.Nz),
                                            including = [:coriolis, :buoyancy],
                                            init = save_closure_without_biharmonic,
                                            overwrite_files = true)

ocean.output_writers[:free_surface] = JLD2Writer(ocean.model, (; η = free_surface);
                                                 schedule = TimeInterval(1days),
                                                 filename = "ocean_one_degree_free_surface",
                                                 including = [:coriolis, :buoyancy],
                                                 init = save_closure_without_biharmonic,
                                                 overwrite_files = true)

sea_ice.output_writers[:surface] = JLD2Writer(sea_ice.model, sea_ice_outputs;
                                              schedule = TimeInterval(1days),
                                              filename = "sea_ice_one_degree_surface_fields",
                                              overwrite_files = true)

We create a land mask and use it to fill land points with NaNs. The grid's bottom_height is stored as a halo-padded OffsetArray, so we take a view of its interior to build the mask.

Nx, Ny, _ = size(grid)
land = view(To.grid.immersed_boundary.bottom_height, 1:Nx, 1:Ny, 1:1) .≥ 0

Toₙ = @lift begin
    Tₙ = interior(To[$n])
    Tₙ[land] .= NaN
    view(Tₙ, :, :, 1)
end

eoₙ = @lift begin
    eₙ = interior(eo[$n])
    eₙ[land] .= NaN
    view(eₙ, :, :, 1)
end

ηoₙ = @lift begin
    ηₙ = interior(ηo[$n])
    ηₙ[land] .= NaN
    view(ηₙ, :, :, 1)
end

heₙ = @lift begin
    hₙ = interior(hi[$n])
    ℵₙ = interior(ℵi[$n])
    hₙ[land] .= NaN
    view(hₙ, :, :, 1) .* view(ℵₙ, :, :, 1)
end

We compute the surface speeds for the ocean and the sea ice.

uoₙ = Field{Face, Center, Nothing}(uo.grid)
voₙ = Field{Center, Face, Nothing}(vo.grid)

uiₙ = Field{Face, Center, Nothing}(ui.grid)
viₙ = Field{Center, Face, Nothing}(vi.grid)

so = Field(sqrt(uoₙ^2 + voₙ^2))
si = Field(sqrt(uiₙ^2 + viₙ^2))

soₙ = @lift begin
    parent(uoₙ) .= parent(uo[$n])
    parent(voₙ) .= parent(vo[$n])
    compute!(so)
    soₙ = interior(so)
    soₙ[land] .= NaN
    view(soₙ, :, :, 1)
end

siₙ = @lift begin
    parent(uiₙ) .= parent(ui[$n])
    parent(viₙ) .= parent(vi[$n])
    compute!(si)
    siₙ = interior(si)
    hₙ = interior(hi[$n])
    ℵₙ = interior(ℵi[$n])
    he = hₙ .* ℵₙ
    siₙ[he .< 1e-7] .= 0
    siₙ[land] .= NaN
    view(siₙ, :, :, 1)
end

Finally, we plot a snapshot of the surface speed, temperature, and the turbulent eddy kinetic energy from the CATKE vertical mixing parameterization as well as the sea ice speed and the effective sea ice thickness.

fig = Figure(size=(900, 750))

title = @lift string("Global 1ᵒ ocean simulation after ", prettytime(times[$n] - times[1]))

axso = Axis(fig[1, 1])
axηo = Axis(fig[1, 3])
axTo = Axis(fig[2, 1])
axeo = Axis(fig[2, 3])
axsi = Axis(fig[3, 1])
axhi = Axis(fig[3, 3])

hm = heatmap!(axso, soₙ, colorrange = (0, 0.5), colormap = :deep,  nan_color=:lightgray)
Colorbar(fig[1, 2], hm, label = "Ocean Surface speed (m s⁻¹)")
hm = heatmap!(axηo, ηoₙ, colorrange = (-1.2, 1.2), colormap = :balance, nan_color=:lightgray)
Colorbar(fig[1, 4], hm, label = "Sea Surface Height (m)")
hm = heatmap!(axTo, Toₙ, colorrange = (-1, 32), colormap = :magma, nan_color=:lightgray)
Colorbar(fig[2, 2], hm, label = "Surface Temperature (ᵒC)")
hm = heatmap!(axeo, eoₙ, colorrange = (0, 1e-3), colormap = :solar, nan_color=:lightgray)
Colorbar(fig[2, 4], hm, label = "Turbulent Kinetic Energy (m² s⁻²)")

hm = heatmap!(axsi, siₙ, colorrange = (0, 0.5), colormap = :greys, nan_color=:lightgray)
Colorbar(fig[3, 2], hm, label = "Sea ice speed (m s⁻¹)")
hm = heatmap!(axhi, heₙ, colorrange =  (0, 4),  colormap = :blues, nan_color=:lightgray)
Colorbar(fig[3, 4], hm, label = "Effective ice thickness (m)")


for ax in (axso, axsi, axTo, axhi, axeo)
    hidedecorations!(ax)
end

Label(fig[0, :], title)

save("global_snapshot.png", fig)

And now a movie:

CairoMakie.record(fig, "one_degree_global_ocean_surface.mp4", 1:Nt, framerate = 8) do nn
    n[] = nn
end
